hints: Add up all the contributions listed in the stem: one from the ring nitrogen, one from each ring carbon, two from the C=O pi bond and two from the amide nitrogen lone pair.
walkthrough:
Count each contributor carefully**
Think of delocalisation as p-orbitals overlapping side by side. The five ring carbons each supply one p electron, that is 5. The pyridine nitrogen supplies one p electron, that is now 6. The $C=O$ $\pi$ bond supplies 2, that is 8. The amide $NH_2$ lone pair supplies 2, that is $5 + 1 + 2 + 2 = 10$.
Final answer: 10 delocalised electrons

hints: Remember the stem says the amide nitrogen lone pair is part of the delocalised system, so ask yourself what shape a nitrogen with three sigma bonds and no localised lone pair adopts.
walkthrough:
See why an amide is not pyramidal**
A normal amine $RNH_2$ is pyramidal with about $107^{\circ}$ because the lone pair repels strongly. Here you are told the lone pair on the amide nitrogen is delocalised into the pi system. That means it is no longer available to repel in the same way, and the nitrogen becomes effectively planar with three electron domains.

Link planar to the angle**
Three domains arranged to minimise repulsion give trigonal planar geometry. The ideal angle is $120^{\circ}$, so the $H-N-H$ angle in the $CONH_2$ group is predicted to be $120^{\circ}$.

hints: To turn $RCOOH$ into $RCONH_2$ you first need a much more reactive acyl derivative, so think what replaces the $OH$ group in step 1.
walkthrough:
Spot the classic two step route**
Carboxylic acids react too slowly with ammonia to give clean amides, so you first convert $RCOOH$ to the far more reactive $RCOCl$. Keep the pyridine ring exactly the same and just change $COOH$ to $COCl$. That is E, the acid chloride.
Final answer: E is nicotinoyl chloride: pyridine ring with $COCl$ in the 3-position, $C_5H_4NCOCl$.

hints: Step 2 converts an acid chloride $RCOCl$ to a primary amide $RCONH_2$, so identify the small nitrogen nucleophile that supplies the $NH_2$ group.
walkthrough:
Add the nitrogen nucleophile**
The $COCl$ carbon is strongly $\delta+$. Ammonia, $NH_3$, attacks it, $Cl^-$ leaves, and after loss of $H^+$ you get $CONH_2$. So step 2 reagent is ammonia.
Final answer: $NH_3$, ammonia (concentrated ethanolic ammonia).

hints: Both reactions hydrolyse the $CONH_2$ side chain only, so focus on what $CONH_2$ becomes when heated with aqueous acid versus aqueous alkali.
Recall that acid hydrolysis gives the carboxylic acid plus an ammonium ion, while alkaline hydrolysis gives the carboxylate salt plus ammonia.
walkthrough:
Keep the ring, change the side chain**
You are told the six membered ring is unchanged in terms of ring opening. So draw the same 3-substituted pyridine in both products and only transform $-CONH_2$.

Acid product**
Heating an amide with aqueous acid hydrolyses it: $$RCONH_2 + H_2O + H^+ \rightarrow RCOOH + NH_4^+$$ So you get nicotinic acid, $C_5H_4N-COOH$. In strong acid the pyridine nitrogen can also be protonated, which is also accepted.

Alkali product**
Heating with aqueous alkali gives: $$RCONH_2 + OH^- \rightarrow RCOO^- + NH_3$$ So you get the carboxylate anion, drawn as $C_5H_4N-COO^-$ with $Na^+$ alongside, sodium nicotinate.

Final answer: With aqueous acid: nicotinic acid, $C_5H_4NCOOH$ (ring N may be shown protonated as $(C_5NH_5)^+COOH$).
With aqueous alkali: sodium nicotinate, $C_5H_4NCOO^-Na^+$, $C_5H_4NCOONa$.

hints: X shows $CONH_2$ has become $CH_2NH_2$, which is reduction of the $C=O$ to $CH_2$, so recall which powerful hydride reagent is needed for amides.
walkthrough:
Recognise a difficult reduction**
Changing $C=O$ in an amide to $CH_2$ to give an amine needs a very strong source of hydride, $H^-$. $NaBH_4$ is too weak for amides. The standard A Level reagent is $LiAlH_4$ in dry ether.
Final answer: $LiAlH_4$, lithium aluminium hydride (in dry ether, followed by acid work up).

hints: Basicity depends on how available the nitrogen lone pair is to accept $H^+$, so compare whether the $NH_2$ lone pair in each compound is localised or delocalised.
Think about the $NH_2$ in X, which is separated from the ring by $CH_2$, versus the $NH_2$ directly attached to the ring in phenylamine or to $C=O$ in nicotinamide.
Decide which delocalisation is stronger, overlap with a benzene pi system or overlap with a highly electronegative $C=O$ group, to place phenylamine and nicotinamide in order.
walkthrough:
Use availability as your ruler**
A base donates a lone pair to $H^+$. The more the lone pair is pulled away by delocalisation, the weaker the base. So look at each $NH_2$ and ask: can its lone pair move away?

X is the strongest base**
In X the group is $Ring-CH_2-NH_2$. The $CH_2$ spacer breaks conjugation, so the nitrogen p-orbital cannot overlap with the ring pi system. The lone pair stays localised on nitrogen, fully available. That makes X an aliphatic-like amine, the most basic.

Phenylamine is in the middle**
In $C_6H_5NH_2$ the nitrogen lone pair overlaps with the benzene pi system and is delocalised around the ring. It is less available than in X, so phenylamine is weaker than X.

Nicotinamide is the weakest**
In an amide $RCONH_2$ the nitrogen lone pair is delocalised very strongly onto the electronegative carbonyl oxygen, giving $C-O^-$ and $C=N^+$ character. This withdrawal is even more effective than delocalisation into benzene, so the lone pair is least available and nicotinamide is the least basic.

Final answer: Basic strength: X (most basic) > phenylamine > nicotinamide (least basic).
Lone pair in X is localised on N and not delocalised, so readily available to accept $H^+$.
Lone pair in phenylamine is delocalised into the benzene ring; lone pair in nicotinamide (amide) is delocalised onto the $C=O$ oxygen even more effectively, so least available.

hints: First work out the molecular formula of nicotinamide, $C_6H_6N_2O$, and note that the M+1 peak is dominated by molecules containing one $^{13}C$ atom (1.1% abundance per carbon).
Set up the proportion: expected M+1 height = M height x (number of carbons x 1.1 / 100), then substitute M = 80.
walkthrough:
Find why M+1 appears**
The M+1 peak is almost entirely due to one $^{12}C$ being replaced by $^{13}C$. Natural abundance of $^{13}C$ is about 1.1% per carbon atom. Contributions from $^{15}N$, $^2H$ and $^{17}O$ are much smaller and are ignored at this level.

Count the carbons**
Nicotinamide has five ring carbons plus one carbonyl carbon, so formula $C_6H_6N_2O$. Total probability is $6 \times 1.1\% = 6.6\%$ of the M peak intensity.

Scale to the given M height**
$$\text{height}_{M+1} = 80 \times \frac{6.6}{100} = 80 \times 0.066 = 5.28$$ So expect a height of about 5.3.

Final answer: Nicotinamide is $C_6H_6N_2O$.
$$M+1 \text{ height} = 80 \times \frac{6 \times 1.1}{100} = 5.28$$
